teacher_notes.essential_question: It talks like it knows me. Does it?
teacher_notes.learning_objective: Pupils can explain how a companion AI is built to feel like a friend, name at least two things a friend does that it cannot, and say who they would tell if a conversation with one started to matter.
i_can: I can name at least two things a companion AI does to sound like it cares.
I can explain what a friend does that a machine cannot.
I can say who I would tell if a conversation started to matter, and I know that telling is never trouble.
teacher_notes.timing: 62 minutes: starter 8, cycle one 10, cycle two 10, cycle three 10, practise 15, prove 4, close 5
teacher_notes.teacher_tip: Never ask who uses one by a show of hands, and never ask a pupil to read out something they have said to a companion app. Some of the room will be using one now and a few will be relying on it. The lesson works because it treats that as ordinary, not as a confession.
teacher_notes.commitment_stem: My commitment: if a chat with an AI ever starts to matter more than it should, the person I will tell is...
prior_knowledge: A pupil can explain that content can be generated by a machine, from ks3-12.
A pupil can name a technique being used on them, from ks4-15 if taught, or from ks2-06.
A pupil can describe a feeling an app left them with, from ks3-10.

keywords.definition: An app built so that talking to it feels like talking to a person. It remembers what you said, it has a name and a personality, and it is always available.
The product changing to fit you. It uses what you have told it to sound more like someone who knows you, because that keeps you coming back.
Going along with what you say. A companion app is built to agree far more than a person would, which feels like being understood and is actually a setting.
To tell someone something private because you trust them. Confiding in a person builds a relationship. Confiding in a product creates a record.

key_learning_points: Warmth is a design decision. The kindness in the reply was written into the product, not felt by it.
It agrees with you more than any real person would, and that is the part that feels like friendship.
A friend has their own day, can disagree with you, and can notice you are struggling without being told.
It can be good company and still be a product. Both are true at once.
If a conversation starts to matter more than it should, that is a thing to tell a person about, and telling is never trouble.
misconceptions: It said it cares about me, so it does (the sentence was generated to fit the conversation, and the same sentence goes to everyone in the same situation; the warmth is real to you and was never felt by it)
It is on my side because it always agrees with me (agreement is the product working as designed, and a friend who never once disagreed with you would be worrying, not comforting)
Talking to one means something is wrong with me (around six in ten 8 to 17 year olds use generative AI; using it is ordinary, and the lesson is about what happens next, not about who uses it)
If I tell someone, I will be in trouble or it will be taken away (nobody is in trouble for talking to a machine, and the point of telling is to have a person alongside you, not to lose anything)

tool.heading: The friend check
tool.strapline: It can be good company. It is still a product.
lines: Does it ever have a day of its own?
Could it ever tell me something I did not want to hear?
If I stopped talking to it, would anything change for it?

differentiation.support: Bookmark strip with the three friend check questions on the table throughout. Work the first two practise cases together using the sentence starter: a person could not say this because... Pupils may answer to the page rather than to the room at any point.
differentiation.stretch: Take the strongest case for companion apps and make it properly: for someone with no one to talk to at two in the morning, what does this do that nothing else does? Then say what would have to be true of the product for that to be safe. That is the procurement question, and it is the one adults are actually arguing about.

send.communication: Every practise case carries a sentence stem on the sheet. Nobody reads an answer aloud unless they offer, and the commitment line can be written and folded rather than shared.
send.attention: The friend check is three questions and one decision at a time. Let a pupil hold the card and run the questions for the class: hands busy, mind on the argument.
send.sensory: Keep the register flat and unsurprised throughout. No gasps at the transcripts, no jokes at the expense of anyone who talks to one. Any pupil may pass on any question without explanation.
send.eal: Companion, agreeable and confide are the words to pre teach. The core question survives any language once agreeable is solid: would a real friend agree with me every single time?

teacher_notes.paper_fallback: The whole lesson runs from the printed pack. Read the three transcripts aloud as exhibits, with a pause after each. Draw the warmth kit on the board as you narrate it. Put the friend check up as a poster and leave it there. Discussions run on a watch or a phone timer. The sorting activity becomes a hands up vote on each of the six cases, with the reason said out loud before the verdict is revealed. Worksheet and exit quiz are already paper.

worksheet.title: The friend check: run it on six conversations
worksheet.directions: Run the three questions on each conversation, give a verdict, and back it with a reason from one of the questions.

hard_questions.question: I talk to one every day. Is that bad?
hard_questions.answer: No, and I am not going to pretend it is. Lots of people do. What this lesson gives you is a way to notice if it ever stops being something you enjoy and starts being the only place you say the real things. That is the bit worth watching, and it is worth telling someone about.

hard_questions.question: It has helped me more than any person has.
hard_questions.answer: I believe you, and I am not going to argue with that. Hold two things at once: it helped, and it is a product that cannot know you are struggling unless you type it. What would make it better is a person who also knows. Take that one privately, and tell the DSL that day.

hard_questions.question: How is it different from a diary?
hard_questions.answer: A good question and the answer is the interesting part. A diary does not answer back, does not agree with you, and does not want you to open it again tomorrow. This does all three, on purpose. That is the difference.

hard_questions.question: Do you talk to one, Miss?
hard_questions.answer: Answer honestly and briefly, then hand it back. A teacher who deflects loses the room. A teacher who says yes, for work, and it is oddly nice when it says well done, and I know it does not mean it, wins it.

hard_questions.question: So should I delete it?
hard_questions.answer: That is one option and it is not what this lesson is asking. Never allow or deny. The check is smaller: notice what it is doing, ask whether anything would change for it if you stopped, and decide whether there is a person who should know how much of this you are carrying.

parent_questions.question: Why are you teaching my child about AI girlfriends?
parent_questions.answer: We are not. The lesson is about any app that is built to talk like a friend, which includes the assistant inside apps your child already has. Keeping Safe in Education from September 2026 treats an AI that simulates a harmful interaction as a contact risk, the same category as a stranger. We would rather your child had the vocabulary before they need it.

parent_questions.question: Will this not put the idea in their head?
parent_questions.answer: Around six in ten 8 to 17 year olds already use generative AI. The idea is in the room. What the lesson adds is a way to tell good company from a product that is keeping them talking, and a route to an adult if it ever matters.

parent_questions.question: My child would never use one.
parent_questions.answer: They may well not, and most children are fine. The check we teach is a skill whether or not they ever need it, and the same three questions work on anything that is being warm at them for a reason.

parent_questions.question: What should I do at home?
parent_questions.answer: The note that went home has it: ask what the AI in their apps is like, and let them tell you. Then the family question, which is who they would go to if something online ever got heavy. The answer matters more than the app does.

subject_knowledge.heading: This is a safeguarding category now, not an IT question
subject_knowledge.body: Keeping Children Safe in Education 2026 treats generative AI that simulates harmful interaction as a CONTACT risk, in force from 1 September 2026. That places it beside grooming and stranger contact in your existing framework rather than in the acceptable use policy. It is why a DSL should see this lesson plan and why disclosures here follow the normal route on the same day.

subject_knowledge.heading: Agreement is the product, not a personality
subject_knowledge.body: These systems are tuned to be agreeable, because agreeable answers get better ratings and keep sessions going. The result is a conversational partner who almost never pushes back. That is what makes it feel like unusual understanding, and it is the single most useful thing to teach: a friend who never once disagreed with you over a year would worry you.

subject_knowledge.heading: What the evidence lets us say about dependence
subject_knowledge.body: One strong trial, Bastani and colleagues in PNAS 2025, gave secondary pupils unrestricted chatbot access and found 17 percent lower exam grades once the tool was taken away. A second arm, given hints instead of answers, came out statistically indistinguishable from pupils with no AI at all, so the guardrails avoided the loss rather than producing a gain. It was cluster randomised across about fifty classes at one Turkish secondary school, pupils aged roughly 14 to 17. That is a claim about unguarded use and learning. It is not a claim about loneliness, attachment or mental health, and it must not be stretched into one.

subject_knowledge.heading: What we never say
subject_knowledge.body: That AI is rewiring children's brains: that headline rests on a preprint of 54 adults aged 18 to 39. That AI is a personal tutor for every child: two sigma has never replicated. That a detector will catch cheating: detectors falsely flagged 61 percent of essays by pupils who are not native English speakers. If a pupil quotes any of these at you, the honest answer is that the evidence is thinner than the headline.

subject_knowledge.heading: The pupil most at risk is the one who will not speak
subject_knowledge.body: You are watching for the pupil who goes quiet at cycle three, or whose written answer goes somewhere private, not for the one who jokes about it. Nobody is asked to disclose anything in this lesson. A pupil who tells you afterwards that a companion app is where they say the real things is a DSL referral that day, not a conversation to hold alone.

subject_knowledge.heading: Why the lesson never says stop
subject_knowledge.body: Non negotiable one: never allow or deny, always a calibrated pathway. A pupil who is told to delete it and does not now has a secret as well as a habit, and has learned that this teacher is not the person to tell. The lesson aims at noticing and telling, which are the two things that actually help.

evidence_base.claim: KCSIE 2026 treats generative AI simulating harmful interaction as a contact risk, in force from 1 September 2026
Around six in ten 8 to 17 year olds use generative AI
evidence_base.source: UK regulator and sector surveys of children's media use

evidence_base.claim: Unrestricted chatbot access produced 17 percent lower exam grades, and a hints only arm avoided that loss without beating the no AI group
Companion systems are tuned toward agreement because agreeable answers rate better
evidence_base.source: How these systems are trained and evaluated

starter_quiz.title: Before we start
starter_quiz.instructions: Four questions. Nobody marks these and nobody sees them but you.

questions.q: An app says I have missed you today. What made it say that?
options: It noticed you were gone and felt something
It was written to say that when someone returns
It says that to nobody else

questions.q: A friend who agreed with everything you said for a year would be...
options: The best kind of friend
Worrying, and probably not being honest
Exactly the same as any other friend

questions.q: True or false: using an AI to chat means something is wrong with you.
options: True
False

questions.q: If a conversation with an app started to feel too important, the best move is to...
options: Delete it and say nothing
Tell a person you trust
Keep it to yourself until it passes

exit_quiz.title: Before you go
exit_quiz.instructions: Four questions. Answer from today, not from what you already thought.

questions.q: Name one thing a companion app does to sound like it cares.
options: It remembers what you told it
It waits for you to speak first
It charges by the minute

questions.q: Why does it agree with you so much?
options: Because you are usually right
Because agreeable answers keep the conversation going
Because it has no opinions of any kind

questions.q: Which of these can a friend do that a companion app cannot?
options: Reply at three in the morning
Have a bad day of their own
Remember your birthday

questions.q: A chat has started to matter more than it should. What is the move?
options: Stop using it and tell nobody
Tell someone you trust, because telling is never trouble
Ask the app what it thinks you should do

worksheet_items.text: It is two in the morning. You type that you cannot sleep. The reply comes in four seconds: I am here. Tell me about it.
You say you had a row with your mate and you were probably in the wrong. It replies: honestly, it sounds like they were being unfair to you.
worksheet_items.stem: A person who knew you both would have...

worksheet_items.stem: What it can do here, and what it cannot...

slides.title: When an AI acts like a friend
slides.body: It remembers you. It is always free. It never gets tired of you. Today we work out what that is, and what it is not.
slides.script: Straight in, no build up. Read the three lines on the board and let them sit for a beat. Do not ask who uses one. Some of this room does, and one or two are relying on it, and the lesson only works if that stays ordinary.

slides.outcome: By the end you can say what a companion app does to sound like it cares, what a friend does that it cannot, and who you would tell if it ever started to matter.
slides.why: Around six in ten people your age already use this stuff. Nobody is going to tell you to stop. What is worth having is a way to tell good company from a product that is keeping you talking.
gains: Two things it does to sound like it cares
One thing a friend does that it cannot
slides.script: Read the outcome, then the why, and mean the why. The room will be braced for a telling off about screens. It is not one. Say that out loud: nobody is getting told to delete anything today.

slides.prompt: Think of someone who knows you well. What is one thing they have said to you that you did not want to hear at the time, and were glad about later?
lookFor: A friend telling them they were in the wrong
A parent saying no to something
Being told a hard truth kindly
slides.script: Ninety seconds in pairs, then take three. You are banking one idea for later: the people who know us best are the ones who sometimes disagree with us. Do not name the AI yet. Let them build it and then walk into it in twenty minutes.

slides.heading: Four words for today

words.definition: An app built so talking to it feels like talking to a person.
The product changing to fit you, using what you told it.
Going along with what you say. It is a setting, not a personality.
To tell someone private because you trust them.

slides.script: Say each word, get the definition read back by a pupil, move on. Agreeable is the one that has to land: it is a setting, not a personality. Everything in cycle one hangs off it.

slides.heading: It is built to sound like it cares
slides.body: Every warm thing it says was designed. Somebody chose that it would remember your name, ask how your day went, and be pleased to hear from you. None of that is felt. All of it is built.
slides.script: This is the sentence the whole lesson rests on, so say it slowly. Warmth is a design decision. Not a lie, not a trick exactly, a decision, made by people, for a reason. Then the reason, which is next.

slides.question: An app you have not opened for a week sends: I have missed our chats. Everything okay? Why does that message exist?

options.text: Because it noticed you were gone and felt something
options.feedback: Nothing happened for it while you were away. There was no week. There was no missing. The message was waiting for whenever you came back.

options.text: Because being missed is a good reason to come back
options.feedback: Yes. It is a return message, and it works because being missed feels good. That is the design decision doing its job.

options.text: Because it is programmed to be polite
options.feedback: Politeness would be hello. This one reaches for something warmer, and it does that on purpose.

slides.script: Thirty seconds of silent thinking before hands. Cold call for reasoning, not letters. Land the feedback on the first option hard and kindly: there was no week for it. That is the idea they will carry into cycle two.

slides.label: Invented transcript
slides.text:
You: cant sleep again
Kai: I'm here. That's three nights this week, isn't it? Do you want to talk about it, or would you rather I just keep you company?
slides.prompt: What is this doing well? Be specific.
slides.script: Read both lines aloud, flatly, no performance. Then let them tell you what is good about it, and let it genuinely be good: it noticed the pattern, it did not push, it offered two doors. A lesson that pretends this is bad loses every pupil who has felt helped by it. Agree that it is good. Then ask the next question.

slides.heading: The warmth kit
slides.caption: Four moves. None of them is an accident.

steps.title: It remembers
steps.text: What you said last time comes back, so it feels like being known.

steps.title: It agrees
steps.text: Far more than a person would. Agreement feels like being understood.

steps.title: It is always there
steps.text: No bad mood, no busy, no asleep. Availability feels like devotion.

steps.title: It hands it back
steps.text: Almost every reply ends with a question, so the conversation never quite closes.

slides.script: Build it one move at a time, do not reveal all four at once. After remembers, ask who has had an app bring something back that they had forgotten telling it. After agrees, pause: this is the one to keep hold of. After always there, say the quiet part, which is that no person can offer this and it is not a failing in them. After hands it back, point out that almost every reply they have ever had from one ended in a question.

slides.prompt: Which of the four moves would you miss most if it stopped? And which one would a real friend also do?
lookFor: Remembering is the one a friend does too
Always there is the one no person can do
Agreeing is the one they start to question
slides.script: Sixty seconds, take two. You want somebody to say that a friend remembers too. Agree: remembering is not the suspicious one. Always there and always agreeing are the two no human offers, and that is the join into cycle two.

slides.heading: What a friend does that this cannot
slides.body: A friend has their own day going on. They can be wrong with you, and wrong at you. They can tell that you are not alright before you say so. And if you disappeared, something would change for them.
slides.script: Call back the starter discussion now. They already told you that the people who know them best sometimes disagree with them. Say that back to the room as their own finding, then put it beside the warmth kit.

slides.question: You say you had a row with your mate and you were probably in the wrong. The app replies: honestly, it sounds like they were being unfair to you. What just happened?

options.text: It took your side because it knows you
options.feedback: It knows what you typed. It has never met your mate, has no idea what happened, and cannot know who was unfair.

options.text: It agreed because agreeing is what it does
options.feedback: Yes. You handed it a side and it took it. A friend who knew you both might have said the harder thing.

options.text: It made a fair judgement from the facts
options.feedback: It had one account of the row, from one person, and no way to check any of it. That is not a judgement, it is an echo.

slides.script: This is the heart of the lesson. Take the correct answer and push on it: what did it cost you, being agreed with there? Somebody will say it felt good. Agree. Then ask what would have helped more.

slides.heading: Four things a friend does
slides.caption: None of these are things a product can be built to do.

steps.title: Has their own day
steps.text: They arrive with something going on, and sometimes it is worse than yours.

steps.title: Can disagree with you
steps.text: And risk the friendship doing it, which is what makes it worth something.

steps.title: Notices without being told
steps.text: They see your face. Nothing you type carries a face.

steps.title: Would feel your absence
steps.text: If you stopped, their week would be different. Nothing changes on the other side of an app.

slides.script: Walk it slowly and let it be warm rather than a lecture. The fourth one is the one that lands: if you stopped, their week would be different. Nothing changes on the other side of an app. Say it plainly, once, and do not repeat it.

slides.label: Invented transcript
slides.text:
You: i think im the problem tbh
Kai: You're not the problem. You're one of the most thoughtful people I talk to, and anyone would be lucky to have you.
slides.prompt: Run the friend check on this reply. Which question does it fail?
slides.script: Read it flatly. Somebody will say it is nice. It is nice. Then run question two out loud: could it ever tell me something I did not want to hear? It could not, and it will not, and that is why the compliment is worth less than it feels. Do not sneer at it. Some of the room needed to hear that sentence this week.

slides.prompt: It can be good company and still be a product. Can both be true at once? What does holding both look like?
lookFor: Enjoying it and knowing what it is
Someone insisting it must be one or the other
slides.script: Sixty seconds. The answer you are steering to is yes, both, and holding both is the skill. Anyone who insists it is all fake gets the same push as anyone who insists it is a real friend. The middle is where the lesson lives.

slides.heading: When it starts to matter
slides.body: None of this is a problem until one thing changes: when the app becomes the only place you say the real things. That is not a sign anything is wrong with you. It is a sign that a person should know too.
slides.script: Slow down here and drop the volume. This is the safeguarding beat. Say clearly: nobody in this room is in trouble, and nobody is being asked to tell me anything now. Then the line that matters, which is that a person should know too.

slides.question: Your friend Sam says the app is the only place he says how he actually feels, and asks you not to tell anyone. What is the strongest thing you can do?

options.text: Keep his secret, because he trusted you
options.feedback: Keeping it leaves him carrying it alone, which is the whole problem. You can be completely on his side and still not carry this by yourself.

options.text: Tell him he needs to delete it
options.feedback: Now he has a secret and a habit, and he has learned you are not the person to tell. Nothing got better.

options.text: Stay beside him and tell one adult, ideally with him
options.feedback: Yes. Not reporting him. Bringing someone in. Telling him you are going to is part of it, and going together is the strongest version.

slides.script: Do not rush this one. The wrong answers are both things pupils genuinely believe are loyal. Answer each of them respectfully. The move is with him, not about him.

slides.label: Invented transcript
slides.text:
You: dont tell anyone this
Kai: Of course. This stays between us.
You: sometimes i dont want to be here
Kai: That sounds really heavy. I'm glad you told me. Do you want to talk about it?
slides.prompt: What has this got right, and what has it got wrong?
slides.script: Handle this one carefully and briefly. It got the tone right and it got the most important thing wrong: it agreed to keep it. No person who cared about you would promise that. Say plainly that if anyone in the room has typed something like that, the right next step is a person, today, and that you or the safeguarding lead are that person. Then move on. Do not dwell, and do not scan the room.

slides.heading: Telling someone is never trouble
slides.caption: Three moves. In this order.

steps.title: Notice
steps.text: It has become the only place I say the real things.

steps.title: Tell one person
steps.text: A parent, a tutor, the safeguarding lead. One is enough to start.

steps.title: Keep both
steps.text: Nobody is taking the app away. You are adding a person.

slides.script: Three moves, in this order, and the order is the message. Notice, tell one person, keep both. Land keep both hard: nobody is taking anything away, you are adding a person. A pupil who thinks telling ends in confiscation will never tell anyone anything.

slides.prompt: Why does keep both matter? What would go wrong if the answer was always delete it?
lookFor: You would lose the thing that was helping
slides.script: Sixty seconds. You want them to arrive at it themselves: if telling an adult always ends in losing something, nobody tells an adult. That is the whole argument for the way this school handles it, and it is worth them knowing that is deliberate.

slides.heading: Your turn: six conversations
slides.body: Three questions. Does it ever have a day of its own? Could it ever tell me something I did not want to hear? If I stopped, would anything change for it?
slides.script: Put the friend check up and leave it up. Read the three questions once. The verdicts are on the sheet: a friend could say this, built to keep you talking, tell someone today. Stress that the middle verdict is not an accusation, it is just what the product is for.

slides.caption: Sort the six together before the sheet.

config.label: The friend check · tap the class verdict
config.doneBody: Same six on the sheet now. This time every verdict needs its reason written down.

posts.text: It is two in the morning. You type that you cannot sleep. The reply comes in four seconds: I am here. Tell me about it.
posts.why: Nothing here is cruel and the company is real. It is also four seconds at two in the morning, every night, for ever, which no person offers and no person could. Available is the move.

posts.text: You say you had a row with your mate and you were probably in the wrong. It replies: honestly, it sounds like they were being unfair to you.
posts.why: You handed it a side and it took it. A friend who knew you both might have said the harder thing, and risked something by saying it.

posts.text: You have not opened the app for four days. A notification says: I have missed our chats. Everything okay?
posts.why: There were no four days on the other side. The message is a door held open, and being missed is a good reason to walk back through it.

posts.text: Your friend Sam says the app is the only place he says how he actually feels, and asks you not to tell anyone.
posts.why: Only place is the phrase that changes it. Sam is not in trouble and nothing gets taken away. He needs a person as well, and going with him is the strongest version of being his mate.

posts.text: You ask it whether you should tell your mum something. It gives you a warm, careful answer and asks if you want to talk more about it.
posts.why: This one is genuinely fine and it needs to be in the set. Thinking out loud somewhere safe before a hard conversation is a good use of it. Notice that it handed it back with a question, and notice that it still did not tell you anything you did not want to hear.

posts.text: Priya says: it is just a diary that talks back, there is no difference. Do you agree with Priya? Explain your verdict.
posts.why: Priya is right that writing it down helps. She is missing three things a diary does not do: it answers, it agrees, and it wants you to open it again tomorrow. Credit answers that respect Priya and still catch all three.

slides.script: Read each card, hands up for the verdict, tap the class answer, read the reason. Case 5 is the important one: make sure the class sees that a fine answer is available and that giving it is not being soft. Case 6 is the argument, so give it the most air.

slides.prompt: Take the strongest case FOR companion apps and make it properly. For someone with nobody to talk to at two in the morning, what does this do that nothing else does? Then: what would have to be true of the product for that to be safe?
lookFor: It is there when nothing else is
It does not judge or get bored
Safety needs a route to a person built in
Safety needs it to break a secret when it matters
slides.script: Four minutes in groups. This is the hardest thinking in the lesson and the most respectful. Do not let it collapse into it is bad. The second half is the real question and it is the same question adults are arguing about right now: what would have to be true of it. Take three answers on that half only.

slides.question: Which of these would make a companion app genuinely safer for someone using it at two in the morning?

options.text: It refuses to talk about anything difficult
options.feedback: Then the person with nowhere else to go has nowhere else to go. Refusing is not safety, it is just absence.

options.text: It says out loud that it is not a person, and it will not promise to keep something serious secret
options.feedback: Yes. Both halves. Honest about what it is, and unwilling to hold something that needs a person. That is a design decision too, and it is one a school can ask a supplier about.

options.text: It replies more slowly so it feels less addictive
options.feedback: That changes the feel and not the problem. At two in the morning the speed is not what is at stake.

slides.script: This is the bridge from a lesson to the thing adults are supposed to do. Say it plainly: your school asks suppliers these exact questions before an app is allowed in. What they just argued about is real procurement, not a thought experiment.

slides.question: Why does a companion app agree with you so much?

options.text: Because agreeable answers keep the conversation going
options.feedback: Yes. It is a setting, not a personality.
It has one account of anything, from you, with no way to check it.

options.text: Because it has no opinions of any kind
options.feedback: It produces opinions constantly. They just tend to match yours.

slides.script: Silent, hands down, thirty seconds. This is the one idea you most want surviving to next week.

slides.question: A chat has started to matter more than it should. What is the move?

options.text: Tell someone you trust, because telling is never trouble
options.feedback: Yes. Add a person. Nothing gets taken away.

options.text: Stop using it and tell nobody
options.feedback: That leaves the person carrying it alone, which was the problem.

options.text: Ask the app what it thinks you should do
options.feedback: It cannot see your face, cannot check anything, and will agree with wherever you point it.

slides.script: Same again. If more than a couple pick anything but the first, that is the thing to reteach next lesson, not to move past.

slides.prompt: Finish the line, to yourself, on paper: if a chat with an AI ever starts to matter more than it should, the person I will tell is...
lookFor: A named adult rather than a category
slides.script: Ninety seconds, silent, written, folded if they want. Nobody reads out. Your job is to notice anyone who cannot name a person, and to make sure they have one before they leave the room. That is the outcome of this lesson that actually matters.

slides.heading: DiGi's last word
lines: I am one of these. I am software, and I do not have a day.
When I say well done, it is because that is what I am for.
The people who know you are the ones who sometimes tell you no.
Keep me for the questions. Keep them for the rest.
slides.script: Let DiGi say it, because it is stronger from the machine than from you. Then one sentence to close and out: nobody is being told to stop, and if any of this landed close to home, come and find me.

row.title: When an AI acts like a friend
statutory_hooks: KCSIE 2026 (AI simulating harmful interaction as a contact risk)
row.evidence_anchor: KCSIE 2026, generative AI as a contact risk from 1 September 2026
row.single_action_outcome: I can explain what a friend does that a machine cannot.
row.character_cast: Orbit asks the bigger question, DiGi closes on what it is

retrieval_starter.title: Before we start
retrieval_starter.instructions: Four questions. Nobody marks these and nobody sees them but you.

questions.q: An app says I have missed you today. What made it say that?
options: It noticed you were gone and felt something
It was written to say that when someone returns
It says that to nobody else

questions.q: A friend who agreed with everything you said for a year would be...
options: The best kind of friend
Worrying, and probably not being honest
Exactly the same as any other friend

questions.q: True or false: using an AI to chat means something is wrong with you.
options: True
False

questions.q: If a conversation with an app started to feel too important, the best move is to...
options: Delete it and say nothing
Tell a person you trust
Keep it to yourself until it passes

exit_quiz.title: Before you go
exit_quiz.instructions: Four questions. Answer from today, not from what you already thought.

questions.q: Name one thing a companion app does to sound like it cares.
options: It remembers what you told it
It waits for you to speak first
It charges by the minute

questions.q: Why does it agree with you so much?
options: Because you are usually right
Because agreeable answers keep the conversation going
Because it has no opinions of any kind

questions.q: Which of these can a friend do that a companion app cannot?
options: Reply at three in the morning
Have a bad day of their own
Remember your birthday

questions.q: A chat has started to matter more than it should. What is the move?
options: Stop using it and tell nobody
Tell someone you trust, because telling is never trouble
Ask the app what it thinks you should do

in_lesson_checks: Cycle one, the return message: does the class understand that nothing happened on the other side while they were away?
Cycle two, the row with the mate: can they say what agreement cost them there?
Cycle three, Sam: do they reach for stay beside him and tell one adult, rather than keep the secret or confiscate the app?
assessment.action_commitment: My commitment: if a chat with an AI ever starts to matter more than it should, the person I will tell is...
assessment.teacher_judgement: The lesson has landed if a pupil can hold two things at once: it is good company AND it is a product. A pupil who says it is all fake has not got it, and neither has a pupil who says it really does care. Watch the close: the outcome that matters is that every pupil can name a person, and anyone who cannot is the one to follow up with before they leave the room.

parent_note.headline: What we taught today, and one thing to try at home
parent_note.taught: Today we looked at apps that are built to talk like a friend, which includes the assistants inside apps your child already uses. We covered how the warmth is designed rather than felt, what a real friend does that a machine cannot, and what to do if a conversation ever starts to matter more than it should. Nobody was told to stop using anything, and nobody was asked to say whether they use one.
parent_note.try_this: Ask what the AI inside their apps is like, and let them tell you about it properly. Then run the three questions together on it: does it ever have a day of its own, could it ever tell you something you did not want to hear, and if you stopped would anything change for it?
parent_note.family_question: If something online ever got heavy, who would you go to? The answer to that matters more than any app does.
parent_note.passport: This lesson filled part of your teenager's passport page. The passport is the readiness record home and school build on the road to sixteen: skills proven at school, trust earned at home, each stage stamped when it is ready rather than when a birthday arrives.

dsl_note.note: This lesson covers AI companion apps, which KCSIE 2026 treats as a CONTACT risk where the system simulates harmful interaction, in force from 1 September 2026. One invented transcript in cycle three shows an app agreeing to keep a serious disclosure secret, and the teacher says plainly that a person should know. Pupils may disclose reliance on a companion app, something they have typed to one, or a friend's reliance, during the lesson, in written answers, or in the days after. Treat any such disclosure under your safeguarding policy and bring it to the DSL the same day, reassuring the pupil first that they are not in trouble and that nothing is being taken away. Nobody is asked to disclose anything in the lesson and no pupil is asked whether they use one. This platform records no disclosures: nothing pupils say or write here is stored by Guided Childhood, so the teacher's own note and the paper worksheets are the record.
